# R2 Digest — Rise of Samuel 1:1–3:21 (lines 3869–5424)
**Coverage:** Full slice read (cache lines 1–1556 = raw 3869–5424). Tsumura NICOT commentary: structural overview of 1 Sam 1–7 and detailed exegesis of 1:1–3:21 (Rise of Samuel as Prophet). Pages ~103–184. Sections: discourse structure of 1:1–2:11; birth/dedication of Samuel (1:1–28); Hannah’s Song (2:1–10); return of Elkanah and contrast of Samuel vs Eli’s sons (2:11–26); man-of-God oracle against Eli’s house (2:27–36); prophetic call of Samuel (3:1–21).

**Source attribution:** All claims below are Tsumura’s positions/readings in this range unless noted as his report of other scholars.

---

## Claims

### Group A — Macrostructure: 1:1–7:17 and Rise of Samuel (1:1–3:21)

### C-R2-01 | Chs. 1–7 as transitional unit from judgeship to kingship
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** First Samuel opens late in the judges period (mid-eleventh century B.C.) against the cultic/moral chaos of Judges 17–21; Yahweh chooses Samuel to appoint Israel’s first kings; chs. 1–7 form a unified whole on the transition from judgeship to kingship.
- **Quote:** "In this dark time in the history of Israel, Yahweh chose as his prophet Samuel, who was destined to appoint the first kings in Israel. Thus, the first seven chapters, chs. 1–7, constitute a unified whole, dealing with the transitional period from the end of judgeship to the new era of kingship."
- **Locus:** [Page 103] / 1:1–7:17 overview
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-02 | Ark story intentionally embedded; pre-Davidic core
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** The ark narrative (4:1–7:1) is intentionally embedded in the Samuel story (1:1–7:17); Tsumura takes chs. 4–6 as pre-Davidic, with final editing of chs. 1–7 possibly early Davidic—not necessarily exilic as Polzin/Birch argue.
- **Quote:** "The present writer is inclined to take the account in chs. 4–6 as pre-Davidic, though its final editing into a wider section, chs. 1–7, could be during the early Davidic era"
- **Locus:** [Page 103] / 1:1–7:17; cf. 4:1a
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-03 | Literary structure ABABBA: rise of Samuel vs decline of Shilonite priesthood
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** 1 Samuel 1–3 contrasts Samuel’s rise with the Shilonite priesthood’s decline in alternating structure ABABBA: (A) birth + Hannah’s prayer 1:1–2:11; (B) sins of Eli’s sons 2:12–17; (A) Samuel and family 2:18–21a + growth note 2:21b; (B) sins 2:22–25 + growth 2:26; (B) man-of-God message 2:27–36; (A) prophetic call 3:1–21. Resumptive repetition: “the boy/Samuel was ministering to/before the Lord” at 2:11a, 18.
- **Quote:** "1 Samuel 1–3 deals with the rise of the prophet Samuel in contrast to the decline of the Shilonite priesthood. This is reflected in the alternating literary structure ABABBA."
- **Locus:** [Pages 103–104] / 1:1–3:21
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[shiloh]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-04 | Darkest times and divine providence preparing individuals
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** With the ark still at Shiloh but soon to be taken by Philistines, Samuel’s call occurs in one of Israel’s darkest hours; God prepares chosen individuals for his plan regardless of outward despair.
- **Quote:** "It was surely one of the darkest times of its history when Samuel was called to be a prophet of the Lord (1 Samuel 3). This teaches us that regardless of how desperate the situation looks outwardly, God is certainly preparing his chosen individuals in order to fulfill his plan and purpose according to his sovereign will and gracious concern for his people."
- **Locus:** [Page 104] / 1:1–3:21 overview
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[shiloh]], [[divine-providence]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R2-05 | Samuel’s birth as kingmaker inaugurating monarchical era
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Samuel’s birth inaugurates a “decisive period” like Moses (Exod 1–2) or Jesus (Luke 1–2); a new monarchical era is brought about by the birth of the kingmaker who will appoint Saul then David, leading toward the House of David and Yahweh worship in Jerusalem.
- **Quote:** "A new era — the era of the monarchy — was brought about by the birth of the kingmaker. … The one who was to be born to her was not only a prophet of Israel but the one who would establish kingship in Israel, appointing first Saul, then David."
- **Locus:** [Pages 104–105] / 1:1–2:11
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R2-06 | Hannah’s Song as hymn to sovereignty, Magnificat prototype; climax of 1:1–2:11
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Hannah’s “song” (2:1b–10) is less thanksgiving for a son than a hymn to sovereign Yahweh and became the prototype of the Magnificat (Luke 1); the birth story climaxes with the song within the unit 1:1–2:11.
- **Quote:** "But, the “song” (2:1b-10) that Hannah prayed is not so much a thanksgiving for the son as a “hymn” to the sovereign God Yahweh, a song which became the prototype of the Magnificat (Luke 1). Thus, the story of Samuel’s birth reaches its climax with the “song” of Hannah in the story unit, 1:1–2:11."
- **Locus:** [Page 105] / 1:1–2:11; 2:1b–10
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-07 | Discourse structure of 1:1–2:11 (SETTING / EVENT 1 / EVENT 2 / TERMINUS)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Verbal-sequence analysis: vv. 1–3 SETTING (Elkanah and two wives); EVENT 1 = Hannah’s prayer and vow (vv. 4–19); EVENT 2 = Dedication of Samuel (vv. 20–28); v. 28 transitions toward TERMINUS at 2:11 with embedded Hannah’s song (2:1b–10). Chapter begins (v. 3 worship) and ends (v. 28 they worshipped) with family worship, focus on Hannah.
- **Quote:** "vv. 1–3 give the background information (“Elkanah and his two wives”: SETTING) for the following two EVENTs, that is, “Hannah’s prayer and vow” (vv. 4–19: EVENT 1) and the “Dedication of Samuel” (vv. 20–28: EVENT 2). And v. 28 is a transition leading toward the TERMINUS at 2:11, with the embedded “Hannah’s song” (2:1b-10)."
- **Locus:** [Page 105] / 1:1–28; 2:1–11
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### Group B — Birth and Dedication of Samuel (1:1–28)

### C-R2-08 | 1:1 MT “one of the Zuphites from Ramathaim” via AXB (no dittography emendation)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** MT ’îš ’eḥād … min-hārāmātayim ṣôpîm is best read as AXB: AB = ’eḥād ṣôpîm (“one of the Zuphites”) interrupted by X = min-hārāmātayim; plural ṣôpîm needs no emendation; “one of the Zuphites from Ramathaim.”
- **Quote:** "it is also possible to see here an instance of the AXB pattern, in which AB: ’eḥād ṣôpîm (one of the Zuphites) is interrupted by the insertion of X: min-hārāmātayim (from Ramathaim) while keeping the relationship between A and B; hence, X modifies A … B as a whole"
- **Locus:** [Pages 106–107] / 1:1
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-09 | Ramathaim/Ramah location; Zuph clan; Ephrathite possibly Bethlehemite stock
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Ramathaim (later Ramah) is disputed (McCarter: Rentis; Eusebius/Jerome variants); name means “two hills”; Zuph is local clan ancestor; ’eprātî may mean Ephraimite or Bethlehemite—Elkanah might be of Bethlehemite stock dwelling in hill country of Ephraim.
- **Quote:** "Elkanah might have been of Bethlehemite stock rather than being an “Ephraimite,” even though he dwelt in the hill country of Ephraim."
- **Locus:** [Pages 107–108] / 1:1
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-10 | SETTING foreshadows narrative; Lord of Hosts as ultimate agent
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Vv. 1–2 introduce Elkanah/Hannah; v. 3 explains annual pilgrimage; mention of Shiloh, Eli’s priestly family, and “Lord of Hosts” (hidden ultimate agent) foreshadows the whole narrative.
- **Quote:** "The mention of Shiloh and the priestly family of Eli as well as the Lord of Hosts, the hidden but ultimate agent of the events, foreshadows the entire narrative to come."
- **Locus:** [Page 106] / 1:1–3
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[1-samuel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R2-11 | ANE heir concern; two wives and tension (Keret, Hagar parallels)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** In ANE lacking an heir meant end of “house” (Keret epic); second wife if first barren was common (Sarah/Hagar); two-wife household produced jealousy; ’aḥat here means “first.”
- **Quote:** "In the ancient Near East, having an heir was very important, for lacking an heir meant the end of one’s “house.” For example, King Keret of the Ugaritic epic, though he had gold and silver, lost all his male children and so his dynasty was about to be extinguished."
- **Locus:** [Page 108] / 1:2
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]
- **Misc flag:** Hannah — no page yet (central figure of ch. 1; Tsumura cites Meyers: narrative “could just as well be called the Hannah Narrative”)

### C-R2-12 | Elkanah’s annual Shiloh visit as family/clan feast, not listed pilgrimage festivals
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Three annual festivals of Exod/Lev not mentioned in 1 Samuel; Elkanah visits once a year (1:7, 21f.); Haran: family/clan feast including women and children; possible link to Judg 21:19 feast of the Lord at Shiloh; sacrifice-to-the-dead theory is “sheer speculation.”
- **Quote:** "Elkanah’s visit to Shiloh was made only once a year (1 Sam. 1:7, 21f.), and according to Haran his annual sacrifice was “a family or clan feast, confined to the family and celebrated by all its members, women and children included.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 108–109] / 1:3
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R2-13 | YHWH ṣebā’ôt as construct chain; first biblical occurrence; Shiloh connection
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** “Lord of Hosts” is a construct chain (cf. Ugaritic il brt, Kuntillet ‘Ajrud “Yahweh of Teman/Samaria”); hosts can be heavenly bodies, angels, armies, or creatures—likely abstract “plentifulness” intensified by plural; first biblical occurrence; may be specially connected with Shiloh sanctuary; Mettinger’s syncretistic origin of the title is highly conjectural, though kingship of Yahweh at Shiloh might be supported by Hannah’s song.
- **Quote:** "This is the first occurrence in the Bible of the phrase. It may originally have been specially connected with the Shiloh sanctuary (also v. 11; 4:4). … Mettinger’s view is highly conjectural, though his view that the kingship of Yahweh was seemingly current in the Shilonite cult might be supported in view of Hannah’s song"
- **Locus:** [Pages 109–110] / 1:3, 11
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-14 | Shiloh geography, Iron Age sanctuary, destruction traces
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Shiloh = Khirbet Seilun [MR177–162], ~20 miles north of Jerusalem; sacred before Iron Age; Israelite religious center in Judges period; yearly feast (Judg 21:19–21); eleventh-century destruction mentioned in Jer 7:12–14; Ps 78:60, with excavation traces.
- **Quote:** "Shiloh, the modern site Khirbet Seilun [MR177–162], is situated 1.5 miles east of the Jerusalem-Nablus (Arabic name for Shechem) road and 20 miles north of Jerusalem. … Its destruction in the eleventh century B.C. is later mentioned in Jer. 7:12–14 and Ps. 78:60, and traces of the destruction have been discovered in excavations."
- **Locus:** [Pages 110–111] / 1:3
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R2-15 | “Priests for the Lord” as narrator’s reservation about Eli’s sons
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Unique phrase kōhănîm laYHWH (vs usual kōhănê YHWH) may express reservation—translating “[acting as] priests for the Lord”; R. P. Gordon: already an “ominous note.”
- **Quote:** "The author may have had reservations about accepting them as “the priests of Yahweh”; hence, the translation [acting as] priests for the Lord may be preferred here."
- **Locus:** [Page 111] / 1:3
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R2-16 | ’appāyim = “two noses” as sacrificial technical term (MT defended; Ugaritic/Emar parallels)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** ’appāyim should keep literal “two noses” as sacrificial-ritual technical term (Barthélemy), not emended to ’epes; Ugaritic ap “nose” with lung as offering; dual may reflect pairs of sheep; Emar: head as favored part; Elkanah gives Hannah two choicest parts as mark of love (preferred over reading that favored Peninnah).
- **Quote:** "It seems best to keep the literal meaning “two noses” and, with Barthélemy, to read the MT form as a technical term of the sacrificial ritual. … It is interesting to note that the Ugaritic ap “nose” appears together with “lung” (npḥ) as an offering to deities in ritual texts."
- **Locus:** [Pages 113–114] / 1:5
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-17 | Shiloh “house/temple” not contradictory with tent tradition; hêkāl can be large tent
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** No textual evidence Shiloh temple was stone; “house” = dwelling without material specification; “Tent of Meeting” (2:22) suggests cloth center with more stable structure around; hêkāl (first OT use, Sumerian É.gal) can denote large tent (Ugaritic/Mari); second-millennium parallels make monarchical-period anachronism unnecessary.
- **Quote:** "there is no evidence in the biblical text that this “temple” at Shiloh was made of stone. … Though one might see in these expressions “anachronistic touches based on conditions existing during the monarchical period,” such an explanation is unnecessary in the light of these second millennium evidences."
- **Locus:** [Pages 114–115] / 1:7, 9; cf. 3:3, 15; 2:22
- **Targets:** [[shiloh]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-18 | Hannah’s vow: performative giving; Nazirite debate; MT lacks explicit Nazirite title
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Vow form common with Ugaritic Keret; “I will give him to the Lord” has performative force (already given by faith); life-long dedication exceeds normal temporary Nazirite (Num 6); explicit Nazirite reference and wine abstinence absent from MT (LXX/4QSama expand); razor phrase may be aposiopesis or infancy-focused; R. P. Gordon’s Samson contrast is secondary to immediate context.
- **Quote:** "The fact remains that explicit reference to the Nazirite is not made and the abstinence from grape products (see Num. 6:3–4) is not mentioned here in the MT."
- **Locus:** [Pages 117–119] / 1:11
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-19 | “Pray before” vs “pray to”; Eli misreads Hannah as drunk
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** “Praying before the Lord” first in OT—emphasizes presence, vs “pray to” implying more distance; Eli misreads quivering lips as drunkenness.
- **Quote:** "Though closer, Eli misread her quivering mouth as the mild derangement of a drunk. … “to pray before the Lord” in the present context is distinct from “to pray to the Lord.” While the former emphasizes the prayer in the presence of Yahweh, the latter emphasizes the direction of prayer, implying more distance from him."
- **Locus:** [Pages 119–120] / 1:12–13
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[shiloh]]

### C-R2-20 | Excursus: bat belîyā‘al as “Daughter of Beliyaal” (underworld queen), not merely “worthless woman”
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** After surveying etymologies (belî+yā‘al; *bl‘ “swallow/destroy”), Tsumura proposes bat belîyā‘al as archaic reflecting stage as DN: “Daughter of Beliyaal” = Queen of underworld (like Eresh-ki-gal); idiom “deliver up to presence of Beliyaal’s daughter” = destroy utterly; fits MT “Do not deliver up your maidservant … to the Daughter of Beliyaal.”
- **Quote:** "I propose that here the phrase bat belîyā‘al is an archaic phrase reflecting the second stage and probably means “the Daughter of Beliyaal,” which refers to the Queen of the underworld, like Eresh-ki-gal of the Mesopotamian tradition."
- **Locus:** [Pages 122–124] / 1:16 Excursus
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-21 | Eli’s blessing “God of Israel” vs Hannah’s intimate YHWH usage
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Eli invokes “God of Israel”; Hannah uses covenant name YHWH frequently; narrator emphasizes Hannah/Elkanah’s personal intimate relationship with Yahweh vs Eli’s formal cultic association; “Go in peace!” marks successful negotiation; only OT place a priest blesses an individual (R. P. Gordon).
- **Quote:** "The narrator seems to emphasize the personal and intimate relationship of Hannah and Elkanah with Yahweh … in contrast with Eli’s formal association with the cult of Yahweh."
- **Locus:** [Page 121] / 1:17–18
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[shiloh]]

### C-R2-22 | “The Lord remembered her” as TERMINUS; Northwest Semitic religious “remembering”
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Stage shifts Shiloh→Ramah (viewpoint *bw’ “came”); Ramah of Benjamin probably er-Rām; “remembering” = benevolent treatment often in response to plea (McCarter); short sentence wayyizkerehā YHWH is TERMINUS of this narrative part.
- **Quote:** "That God remembered means he “fulfilled” his agreed promises. … With the short sentence, And the Lord remembered her (wayyizkerehā YHWH), this part of the narrative ends (i.e., the TERMINUS)."
- **Locus:** [Pages 124–125] / 1:19
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R2-23 | Name Samuel: assonance with *š’l, not etymology; preferred “Name-of-God”
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Association of Samuel with “I requested him from the Lord” is assonance not etymology (cannot be šā’ûl mē’ēl); preferred etymology šemû’ēl “Name-of-God” without emendation; contextually God-given child bears God’s “name/essence”; McCarter’s claim that Samuel’s birth narrative absorbed Saul’s birth account lacks evidence.
- **Quote:** "the association of the two is probably meant to be conveyed by assonance, not by etymology. … But the last view is most natural and does not require emendation."
- **Locus:** [Pages 127–128] / 1:20
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-24 | Elkanah’s “establish his word” = general divine will, not specific promise (MT vs LXX/4Q)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Against NEB/McCarter reading “your vow” from LXX/4QSama: Elkanah means Hannah may do what she thinks best so long as the Lord does his own will; “word” = will of God in general; ’ak restrictive; McCarter’s “as yet no word from Yahweh” inappropriate.
- **Quote:** "what Elkanah is saying is that his wife may do whatever she thinks best, as long as the Lord does his own will (lit., “his word”). Here word refers to the will of God in general rather than a specific divine promise to her."
- **Locus:** [Pages 129–130] / 1:23
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R2-25 | MT “three younglings” defended vs “three-year-old bull” emendation
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** MT pārîm šelōšāh need not be emended to “a three-year-old bull” (LXX/4QSama/Peshitta); word order normal for lists; singular can be collective; pār originally “young (one)” (cf. Judg 6:25; Akk. parru; Ugar. pr/prt); generous lifelong-consecration offering from well-to-do Elkanah; one ephah flour substantial per priestly ratios.
- **Quote:** "However, why should the MT be considered problematic? … So, the animals which Hannah brought to Shiloh were not necessarily adult “bulls,” but the younglings of cows or sheep"
- **Locus:** [Pages 130–131] / 1:24–25
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[shiloh]]

### C-R2-26 | whn‘r n‘r “the boy was young” legitimate; key growth expression
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Against McCarter “unintelligible” and Thenius/LXX/4Q haplography: na‘ar can mean servant of any age under another’s authority; phrase denotes Samuel’s early stage of growth and anticipates 2:11, 18, 21, 26 connecting across Hannah’s prayer.
- **Quote:** "the clause is a key expression, denoting “the boy” Samuel’s early stage of growth; in other words, Samuel began his dedicated life in his extreme youth."
- **Locus:** [Pages 131–132] / 1:24
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R2-27 | Wordplay *š’l: entrust/request; Saul-name form not original Saul birth narrative
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Performative Hi. “I entrust” + Qal “requested from” wordplay; šā’ūl form same as name Saul and formal similarity 1:1//9:1 lead some to posit original Saul birth narrative—unsupported: would require Saul’s youth at Shiloh; common NW Semitic name; many assume Saul birth narrative “when no one in biblical antiquity seems to have thought to devise one for David” (Gordon).
- **Quote:** "Such an association between Saul and Shiloh cannot be supported by the biblical text. … This kind of similarity does not necessarily support literary interdependence."
- **Locus:** [Pages 132–134] / 1:27–28
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-28 | wayyištaḥû as plural “they worshipped”; phonetic spelling
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Context expects plural subjects (Hannah, Samuel, Elkanah); may be shortened phonetic spelling of original 3 m.pl.; agent-defocusing transitional function like v. 25.
- **Quote:** "from a discourse-grammatical point of view, a 3 m.pl. form they worshipped would certainly serve as transitional in the narrative, with agent defocusing"
- **Locus:** [Page 134] / 1:28
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R2-29 | Theological close of ch. 1: prayer, gift, dedication under providence
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Ch. 1 introduces future mother of the kingmaker; believers called to approach God through prayer/worship, receive gift, dedicate it; God guides worshiping lives by plan and purpose even as world darkens.
- **Quote:** "In this initial chapter of the books of Samuel, the future mother of the kingmaker, Samuel, is introduced. … God certainly guides the life of worship according to his plan and purpose."
- **Locus:** [Pages 134–135] / 1:1–28 summary
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[1-samuel]]

### Group C — Hannah’s Song (2:1–10)

### C-R2-30 | Song embedded; TERMINUS of birth story; inclusio framing 1–2 Samuel with David’s songs
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Prayer interrupts flow from 1:28b to 2:11a; song is TERMINUS to birth story; with David’s songs (2 Sam 22; 23) frames entire Samuel narrative as thematic/structural introduction.
- **Quote:** "Hannah’s “song” and David’s “songs” serve as a frame or inclusio around the entire narrative of 1–2 Samuel. Thus, the Song of Hannah serves as “a thematic and structural introduction to Samuel.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 135–136] / 2:1–11
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]]

### C-R2-31 | Genre: hymn of praise / thanksgiving not mere birth thanksgiving; prototype of Magnificat
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Not prayer of supplication but psalm of thanksgiving; subject of barrenness only in v. 5; really hymn to God who reverses fortunes; Magnificat prototype (Luke 1:46–55); fits unequal-struggle motif (Labuschagne); royal-psalm candidate via v. 10b king; ideal introit to early monarchy history.
- **Quote:** "The song, which became the prototype of the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), fits as well into the narrative, as does David’s elegy for Saul and Jonathan in 2 Sam. 1:19–27. … It is really a song of praise, or a hymn, to God who reverses human fortunes by his mighty power."
- **Locus:** [Pages 135–136] / 2:1–10
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[divine-providence]]

### C-R2-32 | Song structure: rondo ABABAC not concentric
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Against Caquot/de Robert concentric analysis: better (1) sovereignty 1b–3; (2) reversal 4–5; (3) sovereignty 6–7; (4) reversal 8a; (3) sovereignty 8b–10a; (4) kingship 10b — rondo form ABABAC.
- **Quote:** "The literary structure is a rondo form (ABABAC) rather than a concentric pattern."
- **Locus:** [Pages 140–141] / 2:1b–10
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-33 | Horn / *rwm theme verb; inclusio with anointed’s horn; introduction to monarchy
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** “My horn rises” // plea to “raise the horn of his anointed” forms inclusio; animal horn = strength/pride (possibly kingship), here Hannah’s dignity; *rwm is “theme verb of the poem” (vv. 1b, 7, 8, 10); Song “perfect introduction to the institution of monarchy in Israel.”
- **Quote:** "The Song of Hannah thus makes a perfect introduction to the institution of monarchy in Israel. … Verbal forms of *rwm (“to rise”) also appear in vv. 7, 8, 10, and the verb is “the theme verb of the poem.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 141–142] / 2:1b, 10b
- **Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]]

### C-R2-34 | Enemies are God’s enemies not personal attack on Peninnah; salvation as victory
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** “Against my enemies” is not personal attack on Peninnah (singular) but against God’s enemies; climax of quadracolon is “salvation” as Lord’s “victory” over enemies.
- **Quote:** "With the expression against my enemies, Hannah is not making a personal attack on Peninnah (s.) here, but “against” God’s enemies. … At the climax of the quadracolon the key word salvation appears, whichhere means the “victory” of the Lord over his enemies."
- **Locus:** [Page 142] / 2:1b
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]]

|---|---|
| **Lines covered** | Full cache file (slice R2); raw **3869–5424**; commentary pages **~103–184** |
| **Claim count** | **69** (C-R2-01 … C-R2-69) |

### Top load-bearing claims
1. **Kingmaker birth / monarchical transition** (C-R2-01, C-R2-05, C-R2-29): Samuel’s birth inaugurates the era of monarchy under divine providence.
2. **Discourse architecture** (C-R2-03, C-R2-07, C-R2-32, C-R2-61): ABABBA rise/decline; SETTING–EVENT–TERMINUS; Song rondo; ch. 3 lack→supply of the word.
3. **Hannah’s Song: sovereignty, reversal, anointed king; Magnificat prototype** (C-R2-06, C-R2-30–42): hymn framing Samuel; first *māšîaḥ*; possible pre-Davidic prophecy of kingship.
4. **Shiloh cult and MT defenses** (C-R2-08, C-R2-13–17, C-R2-25, C-R2-53, C-R2-55): Hosts title, sanctuary nature, AXB philology, three younglings, mā‘ôn adverbial.
5. **Eli house sins → Zadok oracle; Samuel’s prophetic establishment** (C-R2-45–59, C-R2-60–69): cultic abuse, reciprocal-honor judgment, faithful priest Zadok; call narrative; word restored at Shiloh before coming darkness.
